ety.text: Latin *rēgnusnom. Latin rēgnum Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Proto-Italic *-ājō Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -ō Latin rēgnō, rēgnārebor. Old French reignier Anglo-Norman regnerbor. Middle English regnen English reign Inherited from Middle English regnen, from Old French reignier, from the Latin verb rēgnō, and the noun rēgnum. Doublet of regnum. Displaced native Old English rīċe (“a reign”) and ricsian (“to reign”).

ex: England prospered under Elizabeth I's reign.
Throughout history, no single dictator has successfully upheld their reign forever, no matter how powerful they seemed to be.

senses.d: The period during which a monarch rules.
ex: The reign of Victoria was a long one.

senses.d: The territory or sphere over which a kingdom; empire; realm; dominion, etc. is ruled.
ex: And the Fox guileful, and most covetous; / That neither pleased was, to have the reign / Twixt them divided into even twain

senses.d: To exercise sovereign power, to rule as a monarch.
ex: He reigned in an autocratic manner.

Both we will raigne as Conſuls of the earth,
And mightie kings ſhall be our Senators.
The House of Piast reigned Poland from its foundation to 1385.

senses.d: To be the winner of the most recent iteration of a competition.
To be a dominant quality of a place or situation; to prevail, predominate, rule.
ex: Silence reigned, broken only by the hideous screeching of vultures and the sound of a lawn-mower being used in the hospital grounds.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French regne, from Old French regne, borrowed from Latin rēgnum.
Inherited from Old French reignier, borrowed from Latin rēgnāre (“to govern”).

Borrowed from Latin imperāre (“command, govern”); Cf. the dialectal emprar and semi-learned Old Spanish emperar.

phr: in the reign of Queen Dick

ety.text: Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English inforce English reinforce From re- + inforce.

senses.d: To strengthen, especially by addition or augmentation.
ex: He reinforced the handle with a metal rod and a bit of tape.
The right homework will reinforce and complement the lesson!

senses.d: To encourage (a behavior or idea) through repeated stimulus.
ex: Advertising for fast food can reinforce unhealthy dietary tendencies.

ety.text: From r- (variant of re-) + Old French enforcier.
From ri- + inforzare, from Latin re- + Old French enforcier, from forcier, from Latin in- + Vulgar Latin *fortiāre, from Late Latin fortia, from Classical Latin fortis.

es:reforzar.gl: to reinforce, to bolster, to buttress
